title: ⚔️ Chapter boss ⭐⭐⭐: what the guide really claims

questions.prompt: Your book prints a model sentence about Scotland: "Scotland is one of the constituent countries of the United Kingdom. It occupies the northern third of the island of Great Britain and shares a land border to the south with England." Write the same two sentences about ENGLAND. Which imitation keeps the structure of the model AND the map right?

options.text: England is one of the constituent countries of the island of Great Britain. It occupies the southern part of the United Kingdom and shares land borders to the north with Scotland and to the west with Wales.

England is one of the constituent countries of the United Kingdom. It occupies the northern part of the island of Great Britain and shares land borders to the south with Scotland and to the east with Wales.

England is one of the constituent countries of the United Kingdom. It occupies the southern part of the island of Great Britain and shares land borders to the north with Scotland and to the west with Wales.

England is one of the constituent countries of the United Kingdom. It occupies the southern part of the island of Ireland and shares land borders to the north with Scotland and to the west with Wales.

questions.explanation: A model is imitated by holding its three moves still and changing only what the map changes. Move one names the whole a country belongs to, and that whole is a state: a piece of land cannot have member countries, so naming the island there — and then the state where the island should be — turns the imitation inside out. Move two puts the country on the island itself, and England fills the south of Great Britain with Scotland above it. Move three names the neighbours and the side each one is on, and a country with two of them names both: Scotland to the north, Wales to the west. Turn that compass round and England ends up standing where Scotland is; move it across to Ireland and there is open sea where its two land borders ought to be.

questions.prompt: A poster outside a palace reads: "the changing of the guard — one of the world's most spectacular ceremonies". A journalist wants to show that the poster is exaggerating. Which finding would actually damage the claim?

options.text: A ceremony held every March in Bangkok is far more spectacular than this one.
The ceremony lasts forty-five minutes, much longer than most visitors expect it to.
On some winter mornings the ceremony is cancelled because of heavy snowfall.
Writers who rank the world's ceremonies put this one outside their top twenty.

questions.explanation: One of the most spectacular claims membership of a top group, not the top place — so the only way to damage it is to show that the ceremony does not belong to that group at all, which is exactly what a ranking that leaves it far down the list does. Naming a grander ceremony in Bangkok damages nothing: the poster never said there was none above it, and that is why writers of advertisements love the phrase. It sounds enormous and it is almost impossible to disprove. The length of the ceremony and the mornings when snow cancels it say nothing at all about how spectacular it is when it does take place.

questions.prompt: A trainee guide has written this description of the castle: "The castle stands on a rock above the town and was begun in the twelfth century." His teacher asks him to keep both of those facts and rewrite the line so that it PERSUADES. Which rewriting does the whole job?

options.text: You will be standing on nine hundred years of history, up on that rock.
Climb up to the castle before you leave: you will not regret the walk.
Come and see the castle a king built on that rock in the eighteenth century.
The castle, begun in the twelfth century, stands on a rock above the town.

questions.explanation: Persuading is recognised by its direction, not by its grammar: the sentence turns round, faces the reader and tells him what he will get out of it. You will be standing on nine hundred years of history does that with a promise and not one imperative — and it carries both of the facts it was handed, the rock underfoot and the age of the walls. The teacher asked for one thing to change, the job of the sentence, and for the facts to survive. An order to climb up before you leave sells hard and keeps neither of them. An invitation that hands the castle to a king and moves it six centuries forward has stopped rewriting and started inventing. And moving begun in the twelfth century to the front of the line changes the order of the words and nothing else: shuffle a description and you still have a description.

questions.prompt: A guide sums up tomorrow's walk out loud, but not in the order the group will walk it: "The coach park is where the walk ends. We meet under the stone arch on the main square. Once the cathedral is behind us we go down to the botanical garden. The covered market comes before the cathedral, not after it." Put the five stops in the order the group will reach them.

options.text: the cathedral
the coach park
the stone arch on the main square
the botanical garden
the covered market

questions.explanation: Nothing here is numbered and no time is given: the order is carried entirely by four small relational words, and they have to be collected out of the order in which they were said. We meet under the stone arch fixes the start. Comes before the cathedral, not after it puts the covered market second and the cathedral third. Once the cathedral is behind us hangs the botanical garden onto the cathedral, so it comes fourth. And is where the walk ends sends the coach park to the very end, however early it was mentioned. That is how a guide really speaks, and it is how a route has to be rebuilt: listen for before, after, once and ends, not for the order of the sentences.

questions.prompt: A brochure ends on this line: "Every August the festival revives the old town." From that one verb a careful reader learns something about the town in the other eleven months. What?

options.text: The old town stays closed to visitors outside the month of August.
For most of the year the old town is quiet and half empty.
The festival has been held in the old town for a very long time.
The old town was destroyed at some point and has been rebuilt.

questions.explanation: To revive is to bring back to life something that had gone still, so the verb carries its own hidden half: you only revive what was quiet. The brochure never says the town is empty for eleven months — it lets the reader work it out, which is why a careful reader must. Closed to visitors goes much further than the word allows, since a quiet town is still open. Nothing in the verb dates the festival, and nothing in it says a stone was ever knocked down: reviving a town is about its life, not about its walls. Verbs of this kind are worth hunting for in a text, because what they take for granted is often what the writer would rather not print.

questions.prompt:
Here is a whole ad, and nothing else is known about the walk:

CITY WALKS — THE OLD HARBOUR ROUTE
Every day at 9.00 am · Departs from the clock tower, North Gate
Ends at the ferry terminal · About two hours on foot
On the way: the fish auction, the lighthouse, the Sailors' Chapel
FREE — no ticket, no booking

Tick EVERY statement that the ad actually PROVES. Leave the others, however likely they sound.

options.text: The walk is announced for Sundays exactly as it is for weekdays.
The visitor pays nothing at all to take part in the walk.
The group finishes the walk at the point where it started.
The fish auction is going on while the group walks past it.
The group is normally back on the street before midday.

questions.explanation: Every day covers Sunday as surely as it covers Monday, so a walk announced for Sundays is printed in all but name. Free, with no ticket and no booking, settles the price at nothing. And nine o'clock plus about two hours puts the group back on the street around eleven, comfortably before midday — the arithmetic is in the ad, so the ad proves it. The other two are what the reader supplies himself. The walk departs from the clock tower and ends at the ferry terminal, two different places, so it does not come back to its starting point. And on the way: the fish auction proves only that the route passes the auction; whether anything is being sold at nine in the morning is a question the ad never touches. An ad proves what it prints, never what it lets you imagine.
